title: How would you design a URL shortener (short-code generation — counter+base62 vs hashing, collision handling, read-heavy caching, redirect 301 vs 302, custom aliases, analytics, scaling the key space)?
shortTitle: How would you design a URL shortener
topicTitle: How would you design a URL shortener (short-code generation

s1_definition.profdef: A URL shortener maps a long URL to a short, unique code and redirects any request for that code back to the original URL. The core decisions are how to generate the short code, either a monotonic counter encoded in base62 which guarantees uniqueness without collisions, or a hash of the URL truncated to a few characters which can collide and needs collision handling; how to serve the extremely read-heavy redirect path with caching; whether to redirect with HTTP 301 permanent or 302 temporary, which has analytics and cacheability consequences; how to support custom aliases and record click analytics without slowing the redirect; and how to size and scale the key space so codes never run out and the system scales horizontally.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India gives every long, ugly account reference a short, memorable locker number. When a customer quotes the short locker number, a clerk instantly looks it up and points them to the right long reference. The bank must make sure two accounts never get the same locker number, it keeps the busiest lockers' mappings on a fast notepad at the front desk because the same few are asked for constantly, and it decides whether to tell customers "this locker number is permanent, memorise it" or "this is temporary, check with us each time", which changes how often they come back to the desk and whether the bank can see how often each locker is used.
s1_definition.oneliner: A URL shortener is a write-rarely, read-constantly key-value system where you generate unique short codes with a counter in base62 to avoid collisions, serve redirects from cache, choose 301 versus 302 based on whether you want permanence or per-click analytics, and scale the key space with enough code length and sharding.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A URL shortener maps a long URL to a short, unique code and redirects any request for that code back to the original URL. The core decisions are how to generate the short code, either a monotonic counter encoded in base62 which guarantees uniqueness without collisions, or a hash of the URL truncated to a few characters which can collide and needs collision handling; how to serve the extremely read-heavy redirect path with caching; whether to redirect with HTTP 301 permanent or 302 temporary, which has analytics and cacheability consequences; how to support custom aliases and record click analytics without slowing the redirect; and how to size and scale the key space so codes never run out and the system scales horizontally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India gives every long, ugly account reference a short, memorable locker number. When a customer quotes the short locker number, a clerk instantly looks it up and points them to the right long reference. The bank must make sure two accounts never get the same locker number, it keeps the busiest lockers' mappings on a fast notepad at the front desk because the same few are asked for constantly, and it decides whether to tell customers "this locker number is permanent, memorise it" or "this is temporary, check with us each time", which changes how often they come back to the desk and whether the bank can see how often each locker is used.

**One line to remember:** A URL shortener is a write-rarely, read-constantly key-value system where you generate unique short codes with a counter in base62 to avoid collisions, serve redirects from cache, choose 301 versus 302 based on whether you want permanence or per-click analytics, and scale the key space with enough code length and sharding.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the core operation and its traffic shape, because it drives every decision. There are two operations: create a short code for a long URL, which is relatively rare, and resolve a short code to redirect, which is extremely frequent. The system is therefore read-heavy by a huge ratio, so the redirect path must be as cheap as possible, while the create path can afford a little more work. The data model is tiny: a mapping from short code to long URL, plus metadata like creation time, owner, expiry, and click count.

Short-code generation is the central design choice, and there are two main approaches. The counter plus base62 approach takes a globally unique, ever-increasing number and encodes it in base62, the alphabet of digits and upper and lower case letters, which packs a large number into few characters. Its great advantage is that uniqueness is guaranteed by construction, so there are no collisions ever, and encoding and decoding are trivial. The challenge is generating the unique counter at scale without a single bottleneck, which you solve by handing each application server a block of the number range at a time from a central allocator, so servers mint codes locally and only occasionally fetch a new block. The hashing approach instead hashes the long URL, for example with a cryptographic hash, and takes the first few characters as the code. Its advantage is that the same URL naturally maps to the same code and no counter is needed, but its serious drawback is collisions: two different URLs can produce the same truncated hash, so you must detect the collision, by checking whether the code already maps to a different URL, and resolve it, by rehashing with a salt or appending characters until the code is free. Because of this, the counter approach is usually preferred for a clean, collision-free design, while hashing is attractive only when you want identical URLs to share a code.

Collision handling therefore matters only in the hashing approach, and the pattern is check-and-retry: compute the candidate code, attempt to insert it with a uniqueness constraint in the database, and if that specific URL is not what is stored there, generate a new candidate and try again. You bound the retries and you rely on the database's unique index to make the final insert atomic so two concurrent creates cannot both claim the same code. With the counter approach this problem disappears entirely, which is its main appeal.

The read-heavy redirect path is where caching lives. Because the same popular short codes are requested constantly, you put a cache like Redis in front of the database, keyed by short code, holding the long URL. On a redirect you check the cache first, and on a hit you return the redirect immediately in sub-millisecond time without touching the database; on a miss you read the database, populate the cache, and redirect. This cache-aside pattern absorbs the overwhelming majority of reads, so the database handles only cache misses and writes. You set a time-to-live so the cache stays fresh and bounded, and you can pre-warm hot codes.

The choice between HTTP 301 and 302 is subtle and consequential. A 301 permanent redirect tells browsers and proxies that the mapping will not change, so they cache it and future clicks may go straight to the long URL without ever hitting your server again; this is fastest for the user and lightest on your servers, but it means you lose per-click visibility because many clicks never reach you, and you can never repoint that code. A 302 temporary redirect tells clients not to cache the mapping, so every click comes back to your server; this lets you count every click for analytics and lets you change the destination later, at the cost of more load on your service. The usual decision is to use 302 when you need analytics or the ability to change destinations, which is common for marketing links, and 301 only when the mapping is truly permanent and you do not need per-click analytics.

Custom aliases let a user choose their own code, for example a branded short link. You treat the chosen alias as a candidate code and enforce the same uniqueness constraint: if it is free, reserve it; if taken, reject and ask for another. You also validate it against a reserved-word list and a format whitelist, and you keep custom aliases in the same key space with a flag so they do not collide with generated codes.

Analytics must not slow the redirect. You do the redirect first and record the click asynchronously, for example by emitting a click event to a stream like Kafka that a separate consumer aggregates, rather than doing a synchronous database write on the hot path. You capture timestamp, referrer, geo, and device, and you aggregate counts in the background. This keeps the redirect fast while still giving rich analytics, and it is a reason to prefer 302 when analytics matter, since 301-cached clicks never reach you to be counted.

Scaling the key space is a capacity question. The number of distinct codes is the alphabet size to the power of the code length, so base62 with seven characters gives on the order of trillions of codes, which is plenty, and you pick the length to comfortably exceed the lifetime volume with headroom. You scale throughput by keeping the services stateless behind a load balancer, sharding the mapping store by code so reads and writes spread across nodes, and relying heavily on the cache for reads. The counter allocator is made highly available by handing out ranges so it is not on the hot path. Expired or unused codes can be reclaimed to extend the space if needed.

Senior nuances worth stating: prefer the counter-plus-base62 approach for guaranteed uniqueness and allocate ranges per server to avoid a central bottleneck; use the database unique index as the final arbiter of code ownership so concurrency is safe; make the redirect path cache-first and record analytics off the hot path; choose 302 when you need analytics or mutable destinations and 301 only for permanent, analytics-free links; and size the code length from projected volume with headroom so you never face a painful key-space expansion.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India sends customers like Rajesh long, ugly statement and payment-confirmation URLs by SMS, and they are too long and error-prone. The bank wants short, unique codes. This is exactly the short-code generation problem, solved cleanly with a counter encoded in base62 so no two long URLs ever share a code.

Problem 2 — The same few promotional short links are clicked millions of times, and hitting the database on every click would be wasteful. This is exactly the read-heavy caching problem, solved with a cache-aside layer keyed by short code so popular redirects never touch the database.

Problem 3 — The marketing team needs to count every click on a campaign link and sometimes repoint it, while a few permanent internal links do not need analytics. This is exactly the 301-versus-302 decision, solved by using 302 for campaign links so every click is counted and the destination stays changeable, and 301 for permanent links.

Our mini-project builds a compact shortener core. The code allocates unique counters in ranges per server, encodes them in base62, stores the mapping with a cache-aside read path, supports a custom alias with a uniqueness check, chooses 301 versus 302 per link, and records clicks asynchronously. The demo shortens a statement URL for Rajesh and a campaign URL, then resolves them.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/shortener/ShortenerDemo.java
java -cp target/classes com.bank.shortener.ShortenerDemo

# Real API usage:
# create
curl -X POST https://bank.in/api/v1/shorten -d '{"url":"https://bank.in/offers/..."}'
# resolve (the hot path) — a simple GET that returns a 301/302 redirect

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to shorten Rajesh's long statement URL, a campaign URL, and a custom alias, followed by resolve requests for the campaign code.

Step 1: To shorten the statement URL, the server asks its RangeCounter for the next unique number. Because the server holds a pre-allocated block, it mints the number locally without contacting the central allocator, so there is no bottleneck. The number is encoded in base62 into a short code, and because every number is unique the code is guaranteed collision-free.

Step 2: The mapping from the short code to the long statement URL is saved with redirect type 301, because this is a permanent internal link that needs no per-click analytics. The uniqueness is enforced by the store so no concurrent create can claim the same code.

Step 3: The campaign URL is shortened the same way but saved with redirect type 302, because marketing needs to count every click and may repoint the link later. The code and its 302 type are stored.

Step 4: A custom alias "rajesh-loan" is requested. The store attempts to reserve it, finds it free, and saves it, returning success. If it had been taken, the store would reject it and the user would be asked for another.

Step 5: A resolve request arrives for the campaign code. The store checks the cache, misses the first time, reads the database, populates the cache, and returns the long URL with its 302 type. The server records the click asynchronously, not on the redirect path, then returns the 302 redirect. The user's browser follows it to the campaign page.

Step 6: A second resolve for the same campaign code now hits the cache, so it returns in sub-millisecond time without touching the database, and again records the click asynchronously. This is the read-heavy caching benefit in action.

Step 7: Because the campaign link is 302, every click came back to the server and was counted, giving complete analytics. Had it been 301, the browser might have cached the mapping and skipped the server on later clicks, which would be faster but would hide those clicks.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    short bank.in/q0V → Rajesh statement (301 permanent)
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    short bank.in/q0W → campaign (302 temporary, analytics on)
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    custom alias 'rajesh-loan' reserved = true
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    HTTP 302 redirect q0W → https://bank.in/offers/home-loan-diwali
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    HTTP 302 redirect q0W → https://bank.in/offers/home-loan-diwali
2026-10-24 15:11:30 INFO    HTTP 302 redirect rajesh-loan → https://bank.in/offers/personal-loan
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── CREATE (rare) ──
  POST /shorten {longUrl}
    │
    ▼
  RangeCounter.next() ──(local block, no central call)──→ unique id 100000
    │
    ▼
  Base62.encode(100000) → "q0W"  (collision-free by construction)
    │
    ▼
  LinkStore.save("q0W", longUrl, 302)  [unique index = final arbiter]
    │
    ▼
  return short link bank.in/q0W

  ── RESOLVE (constant, read-heavy) ──
  GET /q0W
    │
    ▼
  Cache (Redis) ──HIT──→ longUrl (sub-ms) ─────────────┐
    │ MISS                                              │
    ▼                                                   │
  DB lookup → longUrl → populate cache ─────────────────┤
    │                                                   ▼
    │                                   async: publish click event → Kafka → analytics
    ▼                                                   (OFF the hot path)
  HTTP 302 redirect → browser → longUrl

  ── 301 vs 302 ──
  301 permanent: browser caches mapping → faster, BUT later clicks skip server (no analytics, immutable)
  302 temporary: every click returns to server → full analytics + changeable destination
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A URL shortener is fundamentally a write-rarely, read-constantly key-value system, and I design every part around that traffic shape. There are two operations, creating a short code which is rare, and resolving a code to redirect which is enormous in volume, so the redirect path must be as cheap as possible while the create path can afford a bit more work.

The central decision is short-code generation. I prefer a monotonic counter encoded in base62 because uniqueness is guaranteed by construction, so there are never any collisions, and the only challenge, generating the counter at scale, I solve by handing each server a block of the number range at a time so it mints codes locally without a central bottleneck. The alternative is hashing the URL and truncating, which makes identical URLs share a code but introduces collisions that I would have to detect with a uniqueness check and resolve by rehashing or appending characters, so I use hashing only when shared codes are actually desired. In either case the database unique index is the final arbiter of ownership so concurrent creates are safe.

The read-heavy redirect path is served cache-first. I put a cache like Redis in front keyed by short code, so a hit returns the long URL in sub-millisecond time without touching the database, and a miss reads the database and populates the cache, which means the database only sees misses and writes. The choice between 301 and 302 is consequential: a 301 permanent redirect lets browsers cache the mapping so later clicks skip my server, which is fastest and lightest but loses per-click analytics and makes the destination immutable, whereas a 302 temporary redirect brings every click back so I can count it and repoint the link later, at the cost of more load. I default to 302 when analytics or mutable destinations matter and use 301 only for truly permanent, analytics-free links. Custom aliases go through the same uniqueness check, and analytics are recorded off the hot path by emitting a click event to a stream that a separate consumer aggregates, so counting never slows the redirect. For the key space, base62 with seven characters gives trillions of codes, so I size the length to exceed projected volume with headroom and scale by keeping services stateless, sharding the mapping store by code, and leaning on the cache.

On my project at National Bank of India we shortened long statement and campaign URLs sent to customers like Rajesh. We used a counter plus base62 so codes were collision-free, served redirects from a cache that absorbed the millions of clicks on popular campaign links, used 302 for campaign links so marketing could count every click and repoint them while using 301 for permanent internal links, supported custom branded aliases with a uniqueness check, and recorded clicks asynchronously through Kafka so the redirect stayed fast. The lesson I stress is that the entire design follows from the read-heavy ratio: optimise the redirect to the point of serving it from cache, push everything non-essential like analytics off that path, and pick 301 versus 302 deliberately because it silently decides whether you can even see your traffic.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a URL shortener generates collision-free codes with a counter in base62 using per-server range allocation, serves the read-heavy redirect from a cache-aside layer, chooses 302 for analytics and mutable destinations and 301 for permanent links, records clicks off the hot path, and scales by sizing the code length with headroom and sharding the mapping store.
